title: MA8-14024
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the claimant) and her minor son, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, both citizens of Mexico, are claiming refugee protection in Canada under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). In support of their refugee protection claims, they are alleging the following facts.
The claimant's minor child, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, is basing his claim entirely on his mother's allegations.

At the start of the hearing, the panel appointed XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, as the designated representative of her minor son, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, for the purposes of his refugee protection claim in Canada.

At 16 years of age, the claimant started a common-law relationship with XXXXXXXXXXX XXXX, who had raped her. According to the claimant, she had refused to marry him, even though her parents were forcing her to do so. Three children were born of this relationship, which lasted nine years. No longer able to bear being psychologically and physically abused by XXXXXXXXXXX XXXX, the claimant decided to leave him on XXXXXXX, 1981.
In 1985, the claimant met XXXXXXXXXXXXX, with whom she went to live and by whom she had two children, born in 1989 and 1996. This relationship had its ups and downs, and ended in XXXXXX 2000.

In XXXX 2007, the claimant, who had just gone into business running a XXXX with her brother, hired XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, who became her lover. The claimant noticed changes in XXXXX behaviour; he became very aggressive toward her. The claimant was allegedly the victim of violence, theft and verbal abuse. She allegedly also discovered in the newspapers that, in fact, XXXX was a hitman and a criminal who extorted people, and that he had raped her sisters and participated in some abductions using her vehicles.

XXXX telephoned the claimant to intimidate her after a newspaper published the above facts, making death threats against her, which forced the claimant to go and hide at her aunt's XXXX, where, she claimed, XXXX would find her.

Later, XXXX told her that, to prove to her that he had contacts, even in the United States, he was going to give her a little surprise. The claimant stated that it was then that her son XXXXXXX, who was in Kansas, United States, was beaten by some people XXXX sent.

Fearing for her life, the claimant then decided to leave her country and flew from Mexico City to Montréal, where she arrived on XXXXXX, 2008, accompanied by her sons XXXXXX and XXXX XXXX. They made their refugee protection claims immediately upon their arrival, at the airport.
Before the hearing, one of the claimant's sons, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, withdrew his refugee protection claim in Canada.
In making its decision, the panel took into consideration the Chairperson's guidelines on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.
After hearing the testimony and examining all the evidence in the file, the panel concludes that the refugee protection claims should not be allowed, for the following reasons.

In light of the testimony and the evidence in the file, the panel determines that there is no nexus to any of the five Convention grounds, under section 96 of the IRPA. Moreover, there is no torture under paragraph 97(1)(a), because no pain or suffering was inflicted by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity. Consequently, the analysis will be conducted under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Act. Identity

The identity of the claimants was established to the panel's satisfaction. The principal claimant reported to the authorities, with her Mexican passport and Federal Electoral Institute (FEI) card, both of which were seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC). Photocopies are on file. With regard to the minor child, he went to the authorities with his Mexican passport, which was also seized by CIC. Photocopies of this document are also on file. Credibility

The claimant testified that she lived on XXXXXXXXX, XXXXX, XXXXXXXX, and stated, when the panel asked her, that she did not live with XXXX, adding that he lived at the XXXX that she ran with her brother and that she lived somewhere else, at the address on XXXXXXXX. However, when the immigration officer asked her the same question at the port of entry, [translation] "Did he (XXXX) live with you?," she responded, "yes." The panel pointed out to her that there was a contradiction between what she told the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) at the port of entry and her testimony, and asked her for an explanation. The claimant responded, [translation] "In my country, if a person goes out with someone, I understood at the time, if they were in a relationship with each other and if they were living together." The panel rejects this explanation and deems it not credible. The response provided does not explain why the claimant stated, at the port of entry, that XXXX lived with her, and testified, in the hearing room, that XXXX did not live with her. This undermines her credibility.

The claimant was also unable to explain why, in response to the CBSA officer's question: [translation] "Did you know Mr. XXXX before XXXX 2007?," she stated, "No," whereas in paragraph 11 of her personal information form (PIF), she stated the following: [translation] "In XXXX 2007, I met a young man, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and thought it was a good idea to give him work because I needed someone's help, since my brother had XXXX and was no longer able to work." This is a flagrant contradiction between what the claimant stated at the port of entry and what she stated in her testimony at the hearing. In the panel's opinion, the claimant gave an insufficient explanation for why she told the immigration officer that she did not know XXXX before XXXXX 2007 but testified that she met him in XXXX 2007. This seriously undermines her credibility.

With regard to the date on which she made the decision to leave Mexico: At the port of entry, when the immigration officer asked her, [translation] "When did you decide to leave?," she responded, "Around XXXXXX, 2008," but when that same question was posed to her at the hearing, she responded, "At the end of XXXXXX 2008". The panel pointed out to her that there was a contradiction and asked her to explain the discrepancy between her statement at the port of entry and her response to that same question in the hearing room-when did she decide to leave Mexico. She responded, [translation] "Since I had fled my house many times and my life was in danger, I did not want to stay with him, I cancelled the flight. The exact date I made the decision to leave Mexico was XXXXXX, 2008. It was then that I bought my airplane ticket." The panel rejects this explanation and deems it not credible. The claimant did not make it clear why, at the port of entry, she stated that she decided to leave around XXXXXX, 2008, whereas at the hearing, she stated that she decided to leave at the end of XXXXXX 2008.

Since the claimant was unclear about her goal in coming to Canada, the panel found it prudent to ask her what her intention was in coming to Canada, to which the claimant responded, [translation] "To go to a country where I will have peace of mind." She added, [translation] "We went to an agency to figure out in which country to live, and they told us that there was a special offer for going to Canada, and that we could go there."

When responding to the panel's question aimed at finding out whether she had known, before she came here, that Canada granted refugee protection, the claimant responded, "No" and added, [translation] "When I went to the agency, they talked to me about refugee protection." However, the panel pointed out to her that, at the port of entry, she responded that she had found out that Canada granted refugee protection from a man she met in the waiting room of a lawyer's office and from the Internet. When asked to explain this discrepancy, the claimant responded, [translation] "No, he did not tell me that."

In her response to question 31 of the PIF, the claimant stated that, in XXXX 2007, everything in her house at the XXXX-where XXXX was staying-was stolen. At the port of entry, when the immigration officer asked her, [translation] "Did you contact the local authorities, the police?," the claimant responded, "Yes, twice-once in XXXXX 2007 and once in XXXXX 2008". When the same question was posed during her testimony, the claimant responded, [translation] "After the theft at the XXXX, in XXXX 2007." At the port of entry, the claimant stated that she had evidence of the event in Mexico, whereas in the hearing room, she stated, [translation] "No evidence in XXXX 2007 and in XXXXXX 2008." The panel pointed out to her that there was an inconsistency between her statement at the port of entry and her testimony, and asked her to provide an explanation for it. The claimant responded, [translation] "The first time, in XXXXXX 2007, and since the authorities did nothing, in XXXXXX 2007, knowing where my property was, I went to the authorities, and they did nothing." The panel reminded her that, at the port of entry, she had stated that her evidence was in Mexico. When asked again to explain the inconsistency between the notes at the port of entry and her testimony, she responded, [translation] "I did not say that."

In light of the claimant's testimony, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not provide credible testimony in support of her refugee protection claim. However, although many questions were raised during the hearing about the credibility of the claimant's allegations, the panel is of the opinion that the determinative issue is internal flight alternative. Internal flight alternative (IFA)

Firstly, the panel has to determine whether the claimant has a feasible internal flight alternative; that is, whether there is another part of the country where the claimant and her son would not be subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a risk of cruel or unusual treatment or punishment;1 and secondly, to assess whether it is objectively unreasonable for the claimants to seek refuge by relocating to another part of the country before claiming refugee protection abroad2-in this case, in Canada.

With regard to the first factor, when the panel asked the claimant whether she would be safe if she returned to Mexico and settled in Mexico City, Veracruz or Monterrey, the claimant responded, "No" and added [translation] "Nowhere is safe for me." When the panel asked her why she would not be safe in the suggested locations, she responded, [translation] "The authorities can do nothing in the case of bad people and he (referring to XXXX) is very bad. I do not know why, but he showed me that. He beat me and stole from me, but no one took that into consideration." With regard to how she thought XXXX would go about finding her, she added, [translation] "No, I am not even thinking about returning to Mexico." The panel asked the claimant what she thought were XXXX motivations and reasons for still looking for her today, with the intent of harming her. In response to this question, the claimant stated, [translation] "He told me that if I went against him in any way, he would kill me and cut up my corpse, and that he would find me no matter where I went."

The panel asked the claimant whether she had attempted to relocate while she was in Mexico, she responded, [translation] "I went to my aunt's XXXX, two hours by bus from XXXXX-I do not remember-before my departure, I stayed for three days, and he came looking for me, even though he did not know my address before that date." The panel pointed out to her that, at the port of entry, she had stated that she had wanted to go to Mexico City but that she had changed her route, having seen XXXX. When asked to explain this discrepancy, the claimant responded, [translation] "I was on the way to Mexico City, to take the airplane. What I said was not understood at the port of entry," referring to the allegation that some of what she said had been mistranslated. However, the panel pointed out to her that in her testimony, she stated that she was going to her aunt's place and not to catch the flight. In response to this confrontation, the claimant explained, [translation] "That was when that man was looking for me and kept finding me."

Apparently, the claimant's daughter told her that XXXX had called to find out her address, where she was and that he wanted to find her. The panel examined this part of her testimony and is of the opinion that until this communication with her daughter, XXXX did not know exactly where the claimant was. This casts doubt on the claimant's idea of his capacity and his having contacts everywhere who would help him find her anywhere in Mexico, particularly in the suggested locations-Mexico City, Veracruz or Monterrey.
The panel is not satisfied with the claimant's responses and finds them insufficient as reasons for XXXX' ability or desire to look for her throughout Mexico, particularly in the suggested places.

Moreover, the documentary evidence indicates that the Mexican government has implemented a certain number of prevention and awareness programs, and has made available legal and other resources for people who, like the claimant, fear for their safety. The Mexican federal government has also provided a certain number of services to citizens3 in order to encourage them to report corruption-for example, the electronic system (Sistema de Informacion y Atencion a la Ciudadania (SIAC)), assistance received directly in the internal control offices (Organos Internos de Control (OIC)), etc. After analyzing the general situation in the suggested locations, and taking into consideration the documentary evidence on the resources available in those locations for prevention and intervention as needed, specifically in Mexico City, Veracruz and Monterrey, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant failed to establish to its satisfaction that she has no internal flight alternative in her country, particularly in the suggested locations.

The refugee claimant has the burden of establishing that she has no internal flight alternative to another part of Mexico.4 In other words, she has the burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that she risks being personally subjected to a risk to her life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment anywhere she would settle in her country. In this case, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant has provided no evidence to the effect that her aggressor, XXXX, has the desire or the means to find her anywhere in Mexico.

Consequently, taking into consideration the claimant's testimony and the evidence in the file, the panel concludes that the claimant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities that, if she had to return to Mexico, she would be subjected to a risk to her life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment throughout Mexico.

With regard to the second factor, when asked to state whether there were obstacles in the suggested areas that would make it unreasonable for her and her son to seek refuge there, the claimant admitted that she could live anywhere in her country if it were not for her problems with XXXX. She therefore did not bring up any other obstacles to her settling in Mexico City, Veracruz or Monterrey with her child.

According to the panel, Justice Létourneau's decision5 indicates "...a very high threshold for the unreasonableness test. It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area."

Consequently, in light of the testimony and the evidence on file and taking into consideration all the circumstances, including those specific to the claimant herself, the panel is of the opinion that there is an internal flight alternative for the claimant and her son in their country of origin and that they are not "persons in need of protection" under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

For those reasons, the panel determines that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX are not "Convention refugees" under section 96 of the IRPA or "persons in need of protection" under section 97 of the Act.

Consequently, their refugee protection claims are rejected. Pharès Pierre Pharès Pierre June 2, 2011 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 Rasaratnam v.
